title: Stanford CS221 | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 20: Fireside Chat, Conclusion
transcriptText:
So we're going to have
our fireside chat session.
We're going to have
Percy-- come on.
He's our lovely
instructor for this class.
And we're going to--
let me change this
to this window.
So all of you have submitted a
lot of interesting questions,
and we'll try to hit as
much of them as possible.
But there is a schedule
and there's no guarantee
on what questions we will ask.
But please, there will
be live Q&A sessions
and you can raise
your hand and shout
and I'll signal when that is.
Try not to be too eager
on asking your questions.
So the way this will run is
that we have three sections.
We have career, life,
and research advice.
We have class, Stanford,
and miscellaneous questions.
And then we'll have a section
on AI and its outlooks.
And then we'll go
through them one by one.
And then it'll be more like
a guided interview per se.
OK.
Sounds good?
I mean, we can also go
off script if needed.
So we're doing
something different.
This is a fireside chat.
This is Percy.
Percy, this is a very good way
to get a personal perspective
to Percy and ask questions.
We'll start with the
background introductions.
So what's your first AI class
when you were undergrad?
What did you take?
What did you learn?
Is it similar to 221?
Is it not?
Yeah.
You're asking me to
remember something
from quite a while ago.
Yeah, so I did my
undergrad at MIT.
So I did take the
undergrad AI class there.
I remember it--
I don't remember it being--
at that time I was
much more interested
in theory and algorithms.
So it wasn't like I took
that class and I was like,
OK, I'm going to be an
AI researcher per se.
I think part of
what I remember is
that back then,
machine learning wasn't
as pervasive or
important as it is now.
And so a lot of the more
classical AI techniques,
I could see limitations
in how they could scale.
So I remember taking a class
on NLP and doing grammars,
and we were just
writing grammars
by hand, which didn't
feel very satisfying.
It wasn't until later
during my undergrad
when I did algorithms
and then got
into machine learning and
statistical language processing,
which this was like early 2000.
This is when it first
started, really taking off.
Then I found this is the way to
combine really interesting math
with more scalable
algorithmic approach.
So you mentioned that
there were techniques
like grammar and old techniques
that didn't work as much.
Was there a turning
point where you
were, like, look at
these techniques,
they don't work that well.
You could have switched
to do something else.
And why did you stick
with AI back then?
So, I mean, I got into
AI when I was already
doing machine learning.
In fact, the first
project I did back in 2005
was essentially what you
could call training a language
model that back then, of
course, it wasn't a transformer,
was a Markov model.
And there was a particular
way you train it.
But the idea was the same.
You would take a
large amount of text.
Back then, there was, I
think, maybe 100 million words
instead of trillions of words.
And then you would
maximum likelihood.
It's the same thing
we do now, but
with a different architecture
and a different learning
algorithm.
And at the end of
the day, you get
this model, which
had features, it
would basically
cluster the words.
And I remember seeing how it
would automatically figure out,
here's a cluster of city names,
or here's a cluster of days
of the week and so on.
And that was a moment when I
thought, wow, this is really,
I guess you could call
it emergent capabilities.
And that's why I
decided to go pursue AI.
That's very interesting journey.
10 years later, or even 20
years later, now the world
is very, very different.
Did you expect any of this to
happen, like, language models
to dominate the AI paradigm?
Or were you back then still
thinking about other techniques?
So it's interesting because
even 20 years ago, there
was this idea that
training generative
models on large amounts
of data can be useful.
But I don't think
I-- or really I
think anyone had the imagination
to think that if you just say,
well, I'll just
speak for myself.
But I think most people did not
as well have the imagination
to think that if you just
really stuck with that idea
and carried it to its
logical conclusion
that you would get GPT, GPT 3,
GPT 5, and things like that.
I think that the transition
towards interesting word
clusters to zero shotting a
bunch of different tasks, that
was a pretty major leap that
even I think if you talk
to the OpenAI researchers,
I think there was
a conviction that this was
the path, but whether it came
would come in 2020 versus 2030
or 2050, I think no one knew.
Now's a good time to
transition into AI outlook.
We can ask about what we
think about AI being happening
now, what it's going to
happen in 5 to 10 years,
and we get persistence on that.
So what's one
concrete thing that
changed about all
of this in your mind
when you think about AI systems
in the last three years,
seeing all this happen,
like, maybe before you
were thinking more in perhaps
in terms of principles
and techniques and
algorithms, but right now it's
just data and compute.
Is there anything else that
really drastically changed
your thinking,
seeing this progress?
Well, I think the
big shift, I think
if you think about AI
is that before it was
very much a researcher thing.
AI researchers, they do
a bunch of experiments,
they write papers.
And now, you walk on the street
and everyone's talking about AI.
You drive on the 101,
there's AI billboards.
And it's become not really
about a research thing,
but it's about a
global phenomenon.
I mean, this happens like it
happened with the internet,
for example, as well.
I guess, probably
not many people
were around when
that was happening,
but so that's a big shift.
So I think a lot of
the conversations
have broadened
instead of thinking
about just the techniques
and the principles.
But think about Rishi's
lecture from last time.
You think about data and energy
and compute and resources
and think about jobs and
all these other things,
because AI has escaped the lab
in some sense and has been--
is actually having real
impact in the world
in a very substantial way.
When you have the entire
policy, national policies
being written about
AI, or you have
AI for strategy or
companies calling them,
like, the biggest companies
call themselves AI companies.
I mean, this is a
pretty big shift.
I think it's important to
remember that the research still
continues.
My group, many
people at Stanford
and other universities,
folks in industry,
there's still a lot of
open problems and things
that we don't
understand and things
that could be a lot better.
But that's always been the case
and always will be the case.
It just happens that there's
this off ramp, if you will,
from the research highway
where it's like, oh, OK,
now we can actually get a
bunch of impact here and now as
opposed to always
thinking about the future.
You mentioned a lot of things
here about the role of research
and then the public perception
having billboards on 101.
Let's start with the
public perception,
because we're talking about
how AI is happening today.
What's something that you
think is very correct and very
incorrect about the public
perception of AI today?
When people think
about AI, what's
something that you
want to tell them
that it's the wrong
way to think about it,
or this is the right
way to think about it?
I think a lot of AI
perception, unfortunately,
has been shaped by science
fiction, the Terminator and all
those.
Actually, it's interesting
because in the US also,
it's very cultural.
The way that people think about
AI is very different in the East
than in the West.
I think there's much more
of a dark, bleak outlook
here, whereas in Asia, I think
it's much more of an optimistic,
well, this is a technology
that can really transform.
So that's a first thing
that's interesting.
I personally think that there's
a lot of baggage associated
with science fiction.
And I think things could
be either better or worse,
but in very different directions
than what people typically
think when they're anchored to
the idea of a sentient agent
that comes and either destroys.
I think that-- the
way I think about it
is that AI is
already everywhere.
It's making decisions
much in the background.
So think about it more
as infrastructure,
what recommendations you
get on your phone now.
I think with ChatGPT,
it's more of user facing.
But I think the way that AI will
influence our lives is much more
pervasive, and much of it might
be hidden compared to some AI
walks through the door, right?
That's really good for
movies because it's
hard to have, I don't
know, some abstract thing
walks in the door.
AI working on your spreadsheet--
That doesn't seem
very Hollywood.
On that note, what's the
most overhyped capability
and underhyped capability
of current AIs?
Well, I think I'll start
with the underhyped one.
And this is specific
to language models.
I think we-- language models, if
you think about for much of it
their existence, their
probabilistic distributions
over the next token given
the previous token, right?
So they're mathematical objects
and you can study them as such.
And now, they've transformed
into essentially more
like a system that you've given
an input and you get an output.
So one of the things that
I think is underappreciated
is that how much that
probabilistic view
and how much minimizing
perplexity and having
a strong foundations, it
really enables all of this.
There's a lot of people--
think about it as pre-training
and post-training.
So Ken's lecture, I think,
gave a good overview of that.
And a lot of the visible
things come from post training.
Like you teach the model
how to solve math problems
or do coding or analyze
financial documents
or what have you.
But I think it's
maybe obviously hidden
that many of the things
that make AI tick
is the ability to
predict the next token.
And one way you can
see this is if you
look at the ability
for AI language models
to predict the next token as
a function of sequence length,
like a good system
or a good model,
should really be able to
deeply understand the context
and lower your loss as you
predict the next token,
even to let's say
a million tokens.
And measuring that
loss is something
that really gets at
the true underlying
intelligence or capability of
a system which doesn't really,
I think, show up, I
think, when you look
at these public leaderboards.
That makes sense.
Maybe a overhype thing is--
obviously, a lot of people
are interested in thinking
models and reasoning.
Honestly, if you
look at least, when
I look at some of
these thinking traces,
it just seems like it's a very
long sequence of very rambly,
a lot of inefficiency there.
And yes, you get eventually
to the right answer
and you get good scores.
But it's, like, wow,
this must be a scam
to get you to
generate more tokens.
That's what it feels like.
In fact, even
today, we can't even
be sure that the
thinking-- we don't even
understand how the thinking
traces precisely how the model.
Is it just more
budget, or is it just
actually guiding the thinking?
Sometimes, the thinking
trades can be just wrong,
but still gets you
the right answer.
OK.
Now, let's look
forward a little bit.
You mentioned that there's
still a lot of research to do.
Some people will
agree with that.
Some people will
not agree with that.
In particular, some students may
think that the role of academia
is diminishing, there's
just not too much work
to be done at school because
we don't have the resources.
We don't have the compute.
What do you have--
what are your thoughts on that?
And is AI already solved really?
We have the bulk of it already.
Or are there really more
breakthroughs needed?
Yeah.
So I guess this is
where being older helps.
You can see over
the last 20 years,
I think academia has always been
a very small fraction of what's
happening in the world.
We're always like
this forward thinking,
weird group of people
who do weird things.
And if you look, let's
say even 10 years ago,
or maybe let's say 20 years ago,
and if you were to go at Google
and say like, oh, I have this
really great machine learning
algorithm and we should
use it in search.
So you just know they'll
show you to the exit,
because it was sort of
understood that, well,
these things aren't reliable.
They don't work.
And so, I mean, research has
always been in this position
where it's like barely working.
That's the definition.
And what has happened
over the last five years
is all this very
methods that people
are working on with
scale of course,
and data and compute
start working.
And now there's
a-- now, if you go
to Google, of course
they'll welcome you in.
It's like go work on Gemini.
But there's this-- we're
at a transition period.
And it's not that academia is
being less relevant, but more
that the techniques were
suddenly becoming more relevant.
There's a sense in which
many of the techniques
graduated from school, I guess.
That's kind of apt.
But there's always
more things, like some
of the fundamental questions
about how you can really
generalize well and how do you
become more data efficient.
And all these things are
not solved by any means.
But that doesn't stop you.
And it shouldn't stop people
from trying to productionize
the current best.
So one class of things that
academia is still really
should be doing, I
think, and can be doing
is much more longer term
kind of blue sky research.
I think some the
feeling that you
might get when you
talk to peers is
that they don't see where
that is, because I think
part of the thing is that
the thing that everyone
is looking at, which is
these particular transformer
models, if you follow
them, well, they're
graduating into industry.
But if you're looking
over there, of course,
you're not looking at
the new opportunities.
The other thing, other
class of things, I think
is that the whole class
of problems that academia
is very well incentivized to
do, but industry is just not.
For example, we've been
doing a bunch of work
on understanding copyright.
How much memorized content can
you get out of language models?
So clearly, labs
are not going to go
do this work because they're
already getting sued.
And so any academia, since we
have no skin in the game here,
is the only ones that can
actually do this work.
Or if you think
about evaluation,
how do you evaluate
models in a fair way
or expose problems
with these models?
This is something,
again, which is harder
to do in certain
contexts in industry,
because there's a
conflict of interest.
You have to always be
pushing the capabilities
and showing that
your model is great,
rather than finding
necessarily flaws with it.
Yeah.
That's a very interesting.
On the role of academia, there's
both research and education.
So you touched on a lot
of research problems
that are not yet solved.
But on the education side,
a lot of us are CS students.
We have a lot of
undergrads here.
And one of the things that
students commonly worry about
is that I'm going to graduate
and go into the software
engineering market.
But today, the AI is already
very, very good, software
engineers, they can implement
a lot of things much faster
than the average graduate.
What do you think about that?
And what the role
is of the University
to prepare them
into this market?
Yeah.
So so Rishi showed a nice
slide from last lecture,
which it is true that the
number of entry level software
engineers, as it's currently
defined by the skill set that
has been traditionally the
case for the last 10 years
is going down.
So you can't expect to
just do business as usual,
learn the same, take
the same CS classes,
assuming that they aren't
changing, and just get a job.
I think that this is very
much a transition period where
I, as an instructor and
others in the department
are really trying to figure out
what education and the workplace
should look like.
And it's sort of
a joint problem.
I think at a general
level, I'm not
concerned that people
won't have jobs.
I think that the types of
things you might have to do
will necessarily change.
If you look at previous
generation of technologies,
like from being able to do--
before, if you could do
mechanical computation really
quickly, that earned you a job.
And then calculators came
out and they're like, OK,
you can't get a job by just
like multiplying numbers all day
long.
But that doesn't mean that
there aren't other things to do.
And in fact, I think there's--
once you get the primitives
where oh, yes, I just
have to specify what I
want and the AI will just
write it to freeze
up opportunities
to build other things, right?
In the limit, if you think
about a CEO of a company,
he's probably the
busiest person.
It's not that-- and
there are people
underneath who have many more,
at least technical and maybe
other depth.
In terms of depth,
have way more skills,
but they're still sort of a job.
And not just a CEO, but probably
the whole management chain
of essentially directing
and also deciding what
needs to be done.
So I think long
story short, there's
a shift more towards
from doing to actually
figuring out what to even
do in the first place.
And that is actually a really--
maybe that's one kind
takeaway, is that figuring out
what needs to be
built. Like suppose
you had a tool that could build
any app in like five minutes,
what would you build?
And thinking about that
question, which is not AI,
I mean, that's not
a trivial question,
what app would actually take
off or be useful to people?
That's a very deep question.
So focusing on those
problems, like the people
who can do that well,
are people probably going
to be able to survive
in this new environment.
So you mentioned
finding what to build
is a very important question.
So from your perspective
in the next 5 to 10 years
or even next three years,
what are the application areas
that you think are
undervalued, that people,
that students should think
more about building in?
They have the skill set
of the CS education,
but what should they do?
What's undervalued right now?
Yeah.
I mean, one perspective
is that a lot of AI
is almost synonymous with
these frontier models, which
are essentially everyone
gets exposure to AI
systems like Gemini or ChatGPT.
But I think if you think about
the underlying technology,
the idea of training a
foundation model on tons of data
and unlocking new
capabilities, this
is an incredibly general
purpose technology.
And it could-- you've seen
it successfully applied
to DNA sequences.
And if you think about
the amount of other data
out there, whether it be
climate data or time series,
or other satellite
imagery, there's
many other data sources where
the same type of intuition
should be able to carry over.
And I think there's a lot of--
I think just scratching the
surface of this technology that
can unlock a lot.
So I encourage people
to think outside.
Here's yet another AI
assistant, and think
more about all the
other areas outside CS
and other disciplines in the
sciences, physical materials,
neuroscience, and think about
where there are opportunities
to apply the same techniques.
All right.
We now have a slot
for live questions
if anyone wants
to ask a question.
So the question is, what is
your projected impact of AI?
Is it just a tool or is
it going to be drastically
transform society?
Yeah.
So if you look at Rishi's
slide from last time,
is it the technology
of the year,
the technology of the
decade, or the century,
or I guess, or ever?
I would say, yeah,
century would be my guess.
I mean, I do think
that this is a pretty--
the general purpose nature
is pretty powerful in a way.
I mean, OK, I guess
century-- well,
I think about computing
as a other thing.
Computing was like a
huge deal, and that
was what I got 70 years ago.
So this is probably a
similar magnitude of unlock.
Do current frontier LLMs
pass the Turing test?
If so, what's the next goal?
Has AI been solved
or only scaling
and incremental improvements?
Yeah.
So I mean, I guess
the first thing
to address is whether the Turing
test is the right way to measure
it and how it's defined.
I mean, in terms of--
I think on the first
day of lecture,
I mentioned the
Turing test, and I
think it's historically
been important in many ways
to shape the development.
I think right now,
I don't think it's
a good measure of what it
means, what progress means,
both the imitation part and
also humans being the benchmark.
I think that AI should be--
we want AI to be way better
than humans at certain things.
It should be much more
reliable, for example.
So putting humans at a bar
doesn't seem particularly--
it seems like a bit
shortsighted, I think.
Would there be an
easy-to-understand test,
like a new test, new Turing
test, that you have in mind?
I think in some
sense, it's often
tests are static, which
means that you have to--
you have a system,
it enters a room,
and then you get a score out.
But I think that obviously
has problems because they're
gameable and so on.
I think a better metric is
just in an online sense.
So the way I think
I would propose
is how many new scientific
discoveries is AI producing.
And that is not
gameable, because if AI
cures cancer or invent
some new light material
or figures out fusion or
something, that's going to be--
there's no one can disagree
like, oh, OK, that was cheating.
Because if you cheat it
somehow and you figure out
how to cure cancer,
well, good for you.
Good for you.
Yeah.
All right.
We'll now switch gears to talk
about Stanford and classes
and CS221 in particular.
So we'll start with the class
that you're all in right now.
So when CS221 started 10 years
ago almost, and this year,
we're thinking about
how to make it better.
We're trying to
design it better.
So when you design it trying to
make it better, what were you
thinking?
What problems were
you trying to solve
to make this class better as
an introduction to AI class?
Yeah, yeah.
So there's a few years
along the way where
we've made large changes to the
class, and this was one of them.
And there were multiple
objectives here.
And in hindsight, it was
probably a bit ambitious
in terms of how much
we wanted to do.
But first, thinking more about
the social impacts of AI,
that has always been, as I
mentioned a few minutes ago,
hard to incorporate
because from the ground up,
when I designed this class from
scratch, like 11 years ago,
it was a technical class.
We didn't worry about or think
about the societal impacts
as much.
And so the whole structure
of how the class is built
doesn't really naturally
incorporate that in.
But at the same time, it's
clear that an intro to AI class
needs to confront
some of these issues.
So one of the things we did is
in the latter part of the class,
have dedicated homework
and some lectures to that.
Obviously, this is kind
of work in progress
and we can continue
making it better.
And if you have feedback,
we'd love to hear it.
The other major
thing we did was--
I've always found the
disconnect between lectures,
where you're looking at
abstract diagrams and you--
you look at something
and you think you get it,
and then you go to the homework
and you try to code it up
and you realize,
wait, actually, I
don't understand
how this connects.
And one of the things that
was successful in when
I taught the three 3, 6 class
language models from scratch
is to use this
executable lecture format
where we walk through code.
So there's no ambiguity
about what objects
we're talking about.
And so this year has been a bit
of a pilot in terms of bringing
that format to this class.
Now obviously, there are--
for the first time
something happens,
there's always some rough edges.
So I appreciate everyone's
patience with that.
I do strongly believe
that iterating on this
will produce just a much better
experience, which combines both
of being able to have
intuitive concepts
but also grounded in the code.
So you can see the whole stack.
So 11 years ago, when this class
was designed, to some extent,
we didn't have, quote,
unquote, "working AI."
So AI is a concept.
It seems to be applied
in narrow domains.
But right now, every
one of you have
this ChatGPT, this
UI thing, this cursor
that are actually working.
And we spent a lot of time
on things like search, MDPs,
graphical models, and logic.
And none of that seemed to be
connected to this abstract AI
product that
everyone's using today.
How should students mentally
connect these pieces
to this large language
models paradigm
that we're in right now?
Yeah.
I think as--
hopefully I've tried
to convey that many
of these concepts
are actually quite relevant.
So in search, for example,
we think about states,
and we think about
actions and exploring
different possibilities.
This is exactly what kind of
test time compute with language
models is about.
It turns out that you can't just
train a model and then be done.
There's an inference time
problem of given a model,
how do you search over
different kind of solutions?
And if you think about solving
really, really hard problems,
like, I guess, IMO
problem or just doing
some sort of
scientific discovery,
or doing some data
science problem,
it's going to require trial
and error and that search.
And Markov decision
processes, MDPs, which is--
it's very much like
in language models
when you pre-train
a language model
and then you do
reinforcement learning,
that's basically trying
to learn a policy that
can give you good results.
So that's clearly related.
Any other ones I should defend?
Well, I mean that
covers a lot of them.
But the other part
that we want to cover
is on a more meta level.
CS221 is a introduction to
AI class, but AI is here,
and AI is very productive.
What should such an
introduction to AI class
really prepare
students for, apart
from just concepts
and knowledge?
Is there anything else such a
class should do for students?
Yeah.
I've always been
a strong believer
that you should understand the
fundamentals of how things are
built, and peeling
away the layers,
until you get to the bottom.
I think there's many things you
can do if-- let's say you just
want to get a job, right?
There's many online
resources and tutorials.
You can basically learn
how to do ML engineering
or whatever you want,
and you'll be just fine.
But in some sense,
the whole idea
of having why you're
at Stanford and having
a kind of general education
is the longer term thinking
of both the breadth of topics,
things that you would just never
encounter in the short term,
if you're in a kind of learning
on the job.
But also thinking about a
layer above the kind of,
OK, I need to get this
PyTorch program working.
And so 221 tries to lay out
